This isn't Google related, but I'm also planning to install Debian on an old ThinkPad T42 (until something better comes along), because this whole Windows 10 thing has made me realize just how much I've become the product.

Start with easy concrete steps. Set up your Windows or Mac to dual boot to Linux. Mint works really well for this. Then boot into Linux regularly. When you browse, use Firefox with noscript, adblock, and other privacy settings. Maybe use Google search but log into a throwaway Gmail account to obfuscate who you are. Or use another engine, or alternate between several. For low bandwidth browsing (what you do most of the time) use a VPN service that obfuscates your origin. Always use SSL. Disappearing is hard, far easier to fly low under the radar.

I've spent the last decade or so naively ramming Google (and Microsoft, Dropbox etc.) up my arse and so I'm probably going to spend the next one pulling them back out.

Here's what I'm doing, have done, or am planning to do:

  • Last month, I built myself a cheap Debian Linux server last month (for ~£200; specs here), whis is going to help me with my various plans (see below)
  • I started using a paid VPN, hosted abroad (and not in the US either), to tunnel my internet traffic. It's probably not that effective (yet), but it's a start.
  • I bought a cheap hostname (.moe, specifially) a while back, and I'm going to start a) hosting my own website and b) hosting my own email server (which will give me a fancy email address, too!) Sadly, I'm not sure how to make the switch from GMail, as I've been using that email address for the last ten years or so. This is one of the main things still typing me to Google.
  • I switched from Chrome to Firefox recently, and I can barely find fault with it. The range of add-ons available for it is much wider, too, and I've got several privacy-enhancing ones installed. Again, not ideal when I'm still on Win7, but baby steps.
  • I'm going to start using OwnCloud to make my own alternative to Dropbox
  • I use samba (a Debian package) to allow direct access to my files from my Windows computer.
  • I've started slowly replacing my Skype use with Mumble a lot my my more tech-savvy friends prefer it, it's less resource intensive, has much better audio quality, goes through a server you control, will eventually have video, and uses end-to-end encryption, but good luck convincing your friends to use it. Tox is a more Skype-like alternative, with a specific focus on user privacy rather than just having it as a nice bonus, but suffers the same problem of, everyone's already on Skype.
  • Hopefully, after I've learned enough Linux from the server, I can switch to using a Linux (possbly Mint) desktop. I'm not sure what to do about games though, there are a few solutions (VMs with direct GPU access, WINE, dual-booting) but none of them are satisfactory right now.
  • I'm using DuckDuckGo for web search, and I've found it a mostly acceptable substitute; however, it can get easily tripped up on more complicated queries, and I say a few people today on Voat calling in to question a few things about the company who owns it, which wasn't really enough to convince me. Either way, IxQuick and Startpage (both run by the same company) are viable alternatives, too. Notably, Startpage is the default search engine for the Tor Browser, and DDG is the same for Firefox.

In general, I'd say the best approach towards changing the way you do things is, go at a comfortable pace, and don't try changing everything all at once. A lot of these things take some getting used to (usually because they're just different, not inferior), and the end goal is to find a way to live your life as comfortably as you are used to, but while protecting your privacy and security; and jumping in all at once will just end up making you frustrated and making you wonder if it's all worth it. It is surely worth it, but it's not a goal that can be reached in a day.

The FF extensions I use are: BetterPrivacy (stops supercookies), Blender (stops user-agent tracking), Cookie Monster (cookie whitelisting), HTTPS-Everywhere (by the EFF, searches for and uses HTTPS versions of sites if available), NoScript (JS whitelist), RequestPolicy (a bit annoying to use, but blocks 3rd-party requests), uBlock Origin (adblocker, much better than ABP), and WOT (displays site ratings to help you avoid malware-loaded sites, but has a few privacy implications that I'm still considering).

Feel free to ask any questions if you're curious or ant any more advice! (or to tell me about how all this is pointless because I still use X and it's from Y and they're owned by Z and they like to Q)

Hey guys, we're back again this week with the next installment in our Lords of the Fallen series. I still believe that this game is a bit of a hidden gem, an underrated title that never got much love. Ty and I have been having an absolute blast with it, and I hope that shines through in our videos. For those that don't know, LotF is a game very much in the 'Souls' genre of Action RPG's, but it's generally considered to be the easier, less engaging title of the two series. Still, a lot of thought went into it and Ty and I both consider it to be an awesome game.

We join Ty and James as they continue their journey through Lords of the Fallen. This time, the episode opens to a fight with the game's second boss, the Commander. Using his giant shield and anime sword powers, he attempts to make short work of Harkyn. Unfortunately for him, Harkyn knows the Stab spell.

Upon dispatching the Commander with relative ease, the controller passes from Ty to James. James quickly gets started on the next challenge area, and despite some trouble, makes off with an amazing new faith-scaling staff. With this new staff in hand, James leads Harkyn to victory against multiple opponents.

James also upgrades Harkyn's stab spell, leading to even more insane amounts of damage. Unfortunately, this makes James a bit too cocky, and he's killed by one of the infected. The episode ends with the controller passing to Ty.
